His eyes brightened, and he said:

‘I’ll help you steal him!’

Well, that knocked every thought out of me, like I’d been shot. I’d never heard anything so astonishing, and I have to say Tom Sawyer dropped a long way in my opinion. Only I couldn’t believe it. Tom Sawyer, stealing an enslaved man!

‘Oh, come on!’ I said. ‘You’re joking.’

‘I’m not joking.’

‘Well, then,’ I said, ‘joking or not, if you hear anybody talking about a runaway slave, make sure you remember that you know nothing about him, and neither do I.’

Then we lifted the trunk into my wagon, and he drove off his way while I went mine. Of course, I was so pleased and had so much to think about that I forgot to drive slowly. I got home much too soon for a trip that long. The old gentleman was standing at the door.

‘Well, this is wonderful!’ he said. ‘Who would have thought that mare had it in her? I wish we’d timed her. And there isn’t a drop of sweat on her—not one. Wonderful! I wouldn’t take a hundred dollars for that horse now, I honestly wouldn’t. Before, I’d have sold her for fifteen and thought that was all she was worth.’

That was all he said. He was the most innocent, kindhearted old soul I’d ever met. But it wasn’t surprising: he was a preacher as well as a farmer. Behind the plantation he had a little, insignificant log church that he’d built himself and paid for, to serve as both church and schoolhouse. He never charged anything for his preaching, and that was exactly what it was worth, too. There were plenty of other farmer-preachers down South who did the same.

About half an hour later, Tom’s wagon pulled up at the front stile. Aunt Sally saw it through the window, only about fifty yards away, and said:

‘Why, somebody’s here! I wonder who it is. I do believe it’s a stranger. Jimmy’—one of the children—‘run and tell Lize to set another plate for dinner.’

Everyone rushed to the front door. Naturally, a stranger doesn’t turn up every year, so when one does, he attracts more interest than yellow fever. Tom had crossed the stile and was coming toward the house. The wagon was speeding along the road to the village, and we were all crowded in the doorway. Tom was wearing his store-bought clothes and had an audience, which was always just what Tom Sawyer liked.

Almost a year had elapsed since my father came home, and the seasons had nearly completed their circuit. It was late May; the woods wore their newest green, and the fields were fragrant with freshly cut grass. I hoped that the gentle air and Nature’s lovely countenance would help me awaken softer sensations in him, preparing him through feelings of love and peace for the confidence I was resolved to obtain.

I therefore selected one of these evenings for my endeavour. Asking him to walk with me, I led him into a nearby beech wood, whose airy shade protected us from the dazzling, slanting rays of the setting sun. We walked silently for a while, then sat together upon a mound of moss. Strangely, I seem to behold the place even now. Ivy encircled many of the slender, smooth trunks, its glossy, deep-green leaves contrasting with the white bark and the pale foliage of young beech shoots springing from the parent trees. Moss mingled with the short grass, partly hidden by last autumn’s dead leaves, which the wind had gathered here and there into little heaps. A few moss-covered stumps stood about us. The breeze stirred the leaves softly, and bright blue sky showed through their green canopy. As evening advanced, sunlight reddened the farther trunks and the wind fell wholly still, while a few birds passed on their way to roost.

Here, then, we sat together; and when you learn all that occurred, all the dreadful things that tore our souls even in this peaceful place—which, without strange passions, might have been our paradise—you will not wonder that I remember it so. I gazed upon it hoping its tranquillity would quiet me and lend me persuasive words as well as courage. I saw and absently marked all these details while trying to marshal my thoughts into a suitable order for the attempt. My heart throbbed rapidly as I summoned the strength to address him. I was determined not to allow myself to be rebuffed, yet trembled to imagine the effect my words might produce. At last, with considerable hesitation, I began:

‘My dearest father, your kindness towards me, and the affection—the excessive affection—you showed me when you first returned, will, I hope, excuse my daring to speak to you not merely with a daughter’s tender love, but also with the frankness of a friend and an equal.

I shall dine elsewhere, so I will have no need of you.’

‘Thank you, sir,’ the servant answered as he went out.

‘Now, Alan, we cannot lose a moment. What a weight this chest is! I shall carry it. Bring the remaining things.’ His words came swiftly, with an air of command. Campbell felt himself under his power. Together they left the room.

At the upper landing, Dorian produced the key and turned it in the lock. Then he paused, uneasiness entering his eyes. He trembled. ‘Alan, I don’t believe I can go inside,’ he whispered.

‘That makes no difference to me. I have no need of you,’ Campbell replied coldly.

Dorian pushed the door halfway open. As he did, he caught sight of his portrait’s face leering in the sunlight. The ripped curtain lay on the floor before it. He recalled that, for the first time in his life, he had neglected the previous night to conceal the fatal canvas. He was about to dart forward when a shudder checked him.

What was that repulsive crimson moisture shining upon one of the hands, wet and glittering, as if the canvas had perspired blood? How dreadful it was! For an instant it seemed more dreadful than the silent object he knew lay across the table, whose grotesquely distorted shadow on the stained carpet proved that it had not moved, that it remained exactly where he had left it.

Drawing a deep breath, he widened the opening and hurried in, his eyelids lowered and his head turned aside, resolved not to glance once at the dead man. He bent, picked up the purple-and-gold drapery, and threw it over the entire picture.

There he remained, afraid to turn, his gaze fastening upon the elaborate pattern in front of him. He heard Campbell carry in the weighty chest, the irons, and the other objects needed for his terrible task. He found himself wondering whether Campbell and Basil Hallward had ever met, and what opinion each had formed of the other if they had.

‘Leave me alone now,’ a harsh voice said behind him.

He turned and hastened out, barely registering that the corpse had been pushed back into the chair and that Campbell was staring into a gleaming yellow face. As he descended the stairs, he heard the key turn in the lock.

It was well past seven before Campbell reappeared in the library. His face was pale, but his composure complete. ‘I have carried out what you asked,’ he muttered.
